A retelling is a new version of a story, event, or account that already exists and is already known. Someone takes a story — a myth, a folktale, a novel, a historical event, a religious text — and tells it again, but in a new way.

The word itself is built from two parts you already know: re- (meaning "again") and telling (the act of narrating or presenting something). So literally: telling something again.

The key idea is this: the original exists, and the retelling is born from it. A retelling cannot exist without a source — something it is re-telling.
What makes something a retelling (not just a copy)

A retelling is not a copy. If you simply reproduce a story word-for-word, that is a copy or a reproduction. A retelling must bring something new to the story — a new angle, a new voice, a new setting, a new purpose. Something must have changed.

But at the same time, a retelling is not a completely original, unrelated story either. The core of the original — its plot, its characters, its central conflict, or its essential sequence of events — must remain recognizable. If you change so much that readers cannot recognize where the story came from, it stops being a retelling and becomes an original work.

So a retelling lives between two extremes: it is not a copy, and it is not an entirely new creation. It sits in the middle — deeply connected to the original, yet genuinely transformed.
What can change in a retelling

Almost anything can change in a retelling. Here are the most common things storytellers alter:

The setting. A story set in ancient Greece can be retold in modern New York. A medieval fairy tale can be retold in a futuristic city. The bones of the story stay the same, but the world around it shifts.

The perspective or narrator. A story originally told through the hero's eyes can be retold through the villain's eyes. This is one of the most powerful uses of retelling — it forces us to question who was right and who was wrong in the original.

The language and tone. A dense, classical text can be retold in simple, modern language. A serious myth can be retold with humor. A children's version of a complex story is a retelling.

The characters. Names, genders, backgrounds, nationalities, and personalities of characters can be changed.

The themes emphasized. A story about war can be retold to emphasize the suffering of ordinary people rather than the glory of soldiers. The events stay the same; the lens shifts.

The ending. Some retellings change how a story ends, especially to challenge or question the original's message.

The medium. A novel retold as a film is a retelling. A spoken folktale retold in writing is a retelling.
What must stay the same

For something to remain a retelling (and not become an entirely original work), there must be a recognizable thread connecting it to the original. Readers or listeners familiar with the original must be able to say, "Oh — this is based on that story."

This thread can be:

  • The main plot or sequence of events
  • The central characters (even if renamed or changed)
  • The core conflict or dilemma
  • A distinctive setting or world
  • A well-known theme or moral

Even one strong, recognizable thread is usually enough to anchor a work as a retelling.
The spectrum: from faithful to loose

Retellings exist on a wide spectrum of closeness to the original.

A faithful retelling stays very close to the source. The plot follows the same path, the characters behave similarly, and the events unfold in the same order. The differences might be only in language (simpler, or in a new language) or in medium (a book turned into a film). Children's versions of classic stories are often faithful retellings — the events are the same, but the language is easier.

A loose retelling borrows only the essential shape of the original — maybe its core conflict or a few key characters — and builds something quite different around it. The original is clearly the inspiration, but the new work has gone far in its own direction.

A radical retelling takes only a seed from the original and grows something almost entirely new from it. The connection to the source is real but thin.

None of these is better than the others. All are valid forms of retelling.
Where retellings appear

Retellings appear everywhere across literature, film, theatre, music, and oral tradition:

  • Literature: A novelist retells a Greek myth, setting it in modern-day London and giving voice to a character who was barely noticed in the original.
  • Film: A filmmaker retells a Shakespeare play by moving it to a corporate boardroom with modern characters and dialogue.
  • Theatre: A playwright retells a folktale from the perspective of the monster rather than the hero.
  • Children's books: A picture book retells a complex religious or mythological story in simple language and illustrations for young readers.
  • Oral tradition: Grandparents retelling stories they heard from their own grandparents — slightly changed each time, adapted to the present moment.
Why people create retellings

There are many reasons to retell a story rather than simply create a new one:

To keep old stories alive. Stories from thousands of years ago can feel distant and difficult. A retelling brings them close — into a familiar time, a familiar world, a familiar voice.

To challenge the original. Sometimes a reteller disagrees with the original's message or values. By retelling it, they can question, subvert, or critique it. For example, a retelling might give agency to a character who was passive in the original, or humanize a villain the original dismissed.

To reach a new audience. A story beloved by adults can be retold for children. A story from one culture can be retold for another culture, translated not just linguistically but culturally.

To explore a "what if." What if the story had been seen through different eyes? What if it had happened in a different time? Retelling is a way of asking and answering those questions.

To honor and celebrate. Sometimes a retelling is an act of deep respect — a way of saying, "This story matters so much that it deserves to live again, in a new form, for a new generation."
What a retelling is NOT

It helps to know what a retelling is not, to draw sharp boundaries:

Not a summary. A summary condenses a story and reports it briefly. It does not reimagine or transform. A retelling must actively reshape the story, not merely shorten it.

Not a sequel. A sequel continues a story beyond where it ended — it adds new events that come after the original. A retelling goes back to the original story itself and re-presents it in a new form.

Not an analysis or review. An analysis talks about a story — it discusses its themes, its meaning, its craft. A retelling tells the story itself, just differently.

Not a copy or adaptation in name only. Simply changing a character's name or moving a scene does not make something a retelling. The transformation must be meaningful and intentional.

Not a parody, necessarily. A parody mocks or playfully imitates. A retelling can be playful, but it doesn't have to mock the original — it can be entirely serious and respectful.
Real examples to make it concrete

• "The Lion King" (1994 Disney film) is a retelling of Shakespeare's Hamlet. A prince whose father is killed by his uncle, who then must confront the killer and reclaim his rightful place — the core conflict is the same. But it is set in the African savanna with lions, and the tone is very different from Shakespeare's dark tragedy.
  • "Wicked" (the musical and novel) is a retelling of The Wizard of Oz told from the perspective of the Wicked Witch of the West. Everything you thought you knew is questioned. The villain becomes a complicated, sympathetic character.
  • "Circe" by Madeline Miller is a retelling of Greek mythology from the perspective of Circe, a minor witch-figure who appears briefly in Homer's Odyssey. Miller takes that small character and builds an entire inner life and journey for her.
  • A grandmother telling her grandchildren the story of how their family survived a hard time — but adjusting the details to protect certain people, or to make it more understandable for young ears — is an informal, oral retelling.
How the word is used (collocations)

In practice, "retelling" is almost always used with an adjective that tells you what kind of retelling it is, and usually followed by "of" to name the original:

  • a modern retelling of the Cinderella story — set in present-day times
  • a faithful retelling of the original myth — stays very close to the source
  • a loose retelling of Romeo and Juliet — borrows the idea but diverges significantly
  • a feminist retelling of the fairy tale — told through a feminist perspective
  • a fresh retelling — brings a genuinely new and interesting angle
  • a haunting retelling — emotionally powerful and unforgettable

The noun is countable, meaning you say a retelling (singular) or retellings (plural). You would say: "I read a retelling of the Odyssey last week" or "There have been dozens of retellings of this myth over the centuries."
The essence, in one sentence

A retelling is a new, transformed version of a pre-existing story — recognizably rooted in the original, yet genuinely reshaped in some meaningful way, whether in its setting, voice, perspective, medium, or message.
